When "notwithstanding" is used as an adverb, it means "in spite of that" or "even so" or "all the same."

It is a way of saying: "Yes, there is an obstacle or a difficulty — but the result happened anyway."

Think of it as a word that looks back at something already said and signals that it didn't stop the outcome.
How It Works in a Sentence

As an adverb, "notwithstanding" almost always appears at the very end of a sentence. This is what separates it from its other uses. It points backwards — at the difficulty or opposing fact already mentioned — and says: "Despite all of that…"

Here's the clearest way to see it:

"The roads were completely blocked. They reached the hospital notwithstanding."

Break this down:

  • The obstacle: roads were completely blocked
  • The outcome: they reached the hospital
  • What "notwithstanding" does: it says the obstacle did not prevent the outcome

You could replace it perfectly with: "They reached the hospital all the same." Or: "They reached the hospital even so."
More Examples, Explained One by One

Example 1:

"The critics hated the film. It became a massive hit notwithstanding."

The critics hating it was the obstacle. The film becoming a hit was the outcome. "Notwithstanding" at the end says: that negative reception didn't stop the success.

Example 2:

"She had no prior experience. She was hired notwithstanding."

The lack of experience was the obstacle. Being hired was the outcome. The word tells you: the absence of experience didn't prevent the hiring.

Example 3:

"The plan had several obvious flaws. The committee approved it notwithstanding."

The flaws were the obstacle. Approval was the outcome. Same structure, same meaning: the flaws didn't stop the approval.

Every time "notwithstanding" ends a sentence, it creates a sense of mild surprise or tension. The reader or listener is aware of a difficulty, and the word signals: "and yet, it happened." This is exactly the same feeling as "nevertheless" or "nonetheless," but "notwithstanding" carries a slightly more formal and deliberate tone.

It suits serious, careful writing — legal documents, formal essays, academic work, or careful speech. You wouldn't typically hear it in casual conversation, where people would just say "even so" or "still" or "all the same."
The Exact Synonyms (So You Can Test Your Understanding)

In its adverb form, you can replace "notwithstanding" with any of these without changing the meaning:

  • Nevertheless
  • Nonetheless
  • Even so
  • All the same
  • In spite of that
  • Despite that
  • Still (in formal contexts)

If swapping in one of these feels natural and preserves the meaning, you've understood it correctly.
One Key Nuance: It Refers to the Previous Sentence

The adverb form of "notwithstanding" never introduces new information. It only refers to what came before it. The obstacle is always already stated. The word simply closes the sentence by acknowledging that obstacle and dismissing its power over the outcome.

This is why it sits at the end — it's a conclusion, not an introduction.

Compare:

  • ✅ "The journey was dangerous. He went notwithstanding." — (correct: obstacle stated first, then outcome + "notwithstanding")
  • ❌ "Notwithstanding, he went on the dangerous journey." — (this is the preposition or conjunction form, not the adverb form)
A Simple Test to Recognise the Adverb Form

Ask yourself two questions:

  1. Does the word appear at the end of the sentence?
  2. Is there a previously mentioned difficulty that this sentence's outcome has ignored or overcome?

If yes to both — you are looking at the adverb form, meaning "in spite of that / even so / all the same."
When "notwithstanding" ends a sentence, it means: "There was an obstacle, but it didn't stop this from happening."
